strengths: Clear problem motivation and practical two-step framework addressing the safety-helpfulness trade-off in LLMs
Valuable empirical insight that LLMs can recognize unsafe inputs via prompting but still generate unsafe responses, demonstrating a disconnect between recognition and generation
Systematic ablations investigating classifier architectures, effect of safety prompts, layer-wise representations, and sufficiency of last-token features
Practical focus on lightweight classifiers using publicly available models (Mistral-7B) enhances reproducibility and deployment feasibility
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: single model (Mistral-7B only), single training dataset (WildJailbreak only), and single benign proxy (MMLU-R). No cross-model or cross-dataset generalization studies

Missing end-to-end system evaluation: paper reports isolated classifier performance in Table 1 but never evaluates the complete framework (classifier + safety adapter) on both unsafe and benign prompts simultaneously
Weak baseline comparisons: only Llama-Guard and prompt-based Mistral tested; no comparison with mentioned representation-based methods (PaCE, SEA) or other safety approaches

Insufficient safety adapter analysis: LoRA trained only on WildJailbreak with no robustness testing on new jailbreaks; Figure 1 documents trade-off but proposes no solutions; no mechanistic analysis of adapter modifications

Methodological concerns: harmonic mean balancing two datasets with different properties is crude; linear probing validation uses WJ training data not held-out test set; safety response evaluation method not clearly specified

Critical implementation details omitted for reproducibility: classifier/LoRA training hyperparameters, WJ train/val/test splits, method for determining safe/unsafe responses, and no mention of code release

Claims not well-supported: 'safety at most model stages' based on layer 15+ working well, ignoring poor performance in early layers; 'sequential information unnecessary' conclusion from single overfitting example
Missing practical analysis: no computational overhead assessment, no error analysis characterizing failure modes, no threshold selection guidance for safety-false positive trade-off

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: safety-helpfulness tradeoff in LLMs
Interesting empirical observation that LLMs can recognize unsafe prompts but still generate unsafe responses
Clear presentation and well-motivated introduction
Useful finding that final token representations suffice for safety detection in hidden states
Linear probing analysis (Section 4.2) provides insights into which model layers encode safety information
Practical two-step framework design that could preserve model quality on benign inputs
weaknesses: Critical: Main contribution (two-step framework) is not fully evaluated end-to-end—no results comparing combined system performance to baselines
Severely limited scope: only Mistral-7B tested, only WildJailbreak dataset used; no generalization evidence across models or attack types
No human evaluation of safety; relies entirely on automated metrics which may not capture actual safety
Insufficient experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported
Missing comparisons: does not compare against PaCE, SEA, Safe-RLHF, or other recent safety approaches beyond Llama-Guard
Methodological concern: uses knowledge QA (MMLU-R) as 'safe' baseline, which doesn't reflect real-world safe/unsafe content distribution
Unsubstantiated claims: 'LLMs understand safety' is not well-supported; paper only shows classifiers extract safety signals, not understanding
Reproducibility gaps: minimal hyperparameter details, no code release mentioned, missing LoRA training specifications
No analysis of practical considerations: computational costs, robustness to adversarial examples, false negative risks with 13% jailbreak slippage rate

Missing key experiments: no evaluation on other models (Llama, GPT variants), no adversarial evaluation, no investigation of why safety-inducing prompts fail at generation despite working for detection

strengths: Clear practical motivation: Addresses the genuine safety-helpfulness trade-off problem in LLMs with an intuitive two-step approach
Systematic investigation of design choices: Thorough examination of classifier architectures, input features, and layer-wise analysis with sound experimental methodology
Interesting and actionable insights: Finding that last-token representation alone is sufficient for robust unsafe prompt detection is valuable for practitioners seeking efficient safety mechanisms
Well-designed focused experiments: Good choice of datasets (WildJailbreak for adversarial inputs, MMLU-Redux for benign queries) and clear visualization of trade-offs (Figure 1)
Interpretability contributions: Layer-wise linear probing analysis showing safety information distributed from mid-layers (layer 15+) onward provides useful insights into LLM internals
Clear presentation: Well-written paper that is easy to follow with good motivation and intuitive explanations of methodology and findings
weaknesses: Critical limitation—single model evaluation only: All experiments use Mistral-7B exclusively with no evaluation on other architectures, sizes, or alignment approaches. Findings (e.g., last-token sufficiency) may be architecture-specific and may not generalize across diverse models, severely limiting generalizability claims for ICML standards

Incomplete evaluation of the proposed two-step pipeline: Paper focuses heavily on classifier design but lacks comprehensive end-to-end system evaluation, missing direct comparison with other recent safety approaches and ablation studies of the full framework

Limited dataset diversity: Evaluation restricted to WildJailbreak and MMLU-Redux only. No testing on other jailbreak benchmarks, emerging attack types, or out-of-distribution safety datasets raises questions about robustness and real-world applicability

Reproducibility concerns with missing implementation details: No code availability mentioned, critical hyperparameters absent (learning rates, batch sizes, epochs, early stopping), WJ dataset split unclear, and unclear if results averaged over multiple seeds. Linear probing 'validation sub-sample from WJ training data' is methodologically concerning (should use held-out test set)

Insufficient statistical rigor: Table 1 lacks error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Claims about 'no significant performance gains' (safety prompts) lack formal justification. Figure 1 error bars unexplained

Superficial analysis of core findings: Why [/INST] token is so informative (Mistral-specific?) and how it generalizes to other prompting formats unclear. Disconnect between Mistral's strong safety-prompt detection (0.84) yet minimal MLP improvement deserves deeper analysis. Transformer underperformance (0.85 MMLU-R) suggests overfitting but uninvestigated

Missing critical generalization experiments: No evaluation on out-of-distribution unsafe prompts, cross-model classifier transfer, sensitivity to training data size, computational overhead analysis, or adversarial robustness of the classifier itself

Limited methodological novelty: Core idea of conditional routing to safety adapters is straightforward. Linear probing is standard. Contribution is primarily empirical/engineering-focused rather than introducing novel methods or theory

Incomplete limitation discussion: No discussion of adversarial attacks targeting the classifier, quantified computational overhead, societal impacts of false negatives/positives, or in-depth analysis of generalization failures

Evaluation metric limitations: Accuracy alone insufficient for context-dependent safety preferences. No precision-recall curves, ROC analysis, or discussion of practical trade-offs between false positives and false negatives

strengths: Clear demonstration that instruction-tuned LLMs can identify unsafe prompts yet still produce harmful outputs, revealing an interesting gap between internal representations and observable behavior
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 safety benchmarks and 7 capability benchmarks with multiple model families and sizes
Practical contribution of a training-free, flexible moderation method that works across model families and enables easy adaptation via hierarchical prototypes
Thorough ablation studies examining layer selection, sample size effects, and distance metric choices
Well-executed experimental design with proper reporting of both F1 scores on harmful data and true negative rates on neutral data
Efficient implementation with negligible computational overhead
Good presentation quality with clear visualizations and comprehensive appendix including all prompts
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core technique (Mahalanobis distance-based prototype classification) applies well-established methods to a new domain without significant innovation

Overclaimed framing about LLM 'understanding': the evidence shows safe/unsafe examples cluster differently in latent space but doesn't rigorously establish genuine understanding vs. statistical artifacts from alignment training
Missing critical baseline comparison with simple prompting: Section 3.2 demonstrates prompting can be competitive with the right prompt, but a fair head-to-head comparison with LPM is not provided
Insufficient theoretical justification for why Mahalanobis distance is particularly suited to LLM latent spaces; Gaussian distribution assumption is not verified empirically
Limited scope to input moderation only; no evaluation on completely novel threat types not represented in training prototypes
Modest improvements with hierarchical prototypes (2-4%) requiring manual annotation; cross-dataset generalization not systematically tested
Failure mode analysis (Appendix C) identifies problematic categories but lacks deep investigation into underlying causes
Reproducibility concerns: no mention of code release, train/test split procedures not fully specified, hierarchical prototype clustering details incomplete

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 harmful and 7 neutral datasets with multiple ablations (distance metrics, layer depth, data size, covariance structure)
Interesting empirical observation that models recognize harmful prompts when explicitly queried but still produce harmful outputs without prompting
Practical lightweight method with negligible inference overhead that works across model families and sizes without training new models
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figure 1a showing latent space separation) and thorough appendix with detailed results and prompts
Hierarchical prototype extension enabling extensibility to new harm categories without retraining
weaknesses: Overclaimed central claims: The paper claims LLMs 'understand' safety and 'encode safety-relevant information,' but only demonstrates spatial separation—which could reflect incidental training data correlations rather than genuine semantic understanding

Misleading 'training-free' framing: The method requires labeled safety training data for prototypes. If such data is available, practitioners should question the advantage over training a classifier or using existing guard models

Marginal practical improvements: LPM-M(OLMo2) achieves 89.44% F1 vs. WildGuard's 88.93% (0.51 point difference), within noise margins with no significance testing despite evident variance across datasets

Limited technical novelty: Mahalanobis distance-based prototype classification is established in classical ML; applying it to LLM latent spaces is straightforward application work without novel algorithmic contributions

Critical gaps in methodology: (1) Unclear train/test split for WildGuardMix prototypes with potential data leakage; (2) No comparison to simple baselines (e.g., logistic regression on same representations); (3) Prompting experiment (Section 3.1) lacks rigorous quantification of recognition rates with TPR/FPR analysis
Significant failure on subtle harms: 25% error rate on 'Social Stereotypes and Unfair Discrimination' (Appendix C)—precisely where safety systems must be most reliable—with no proposed solutions

Incomplete generalization analysis: Method requires labeled data for new harm types; sequential improvements (Figure 4b) essentially show retraining, not true generalization to novel harms. No evaluation on truly out-of-distribution harm types

Missing technical justification: (1) No explanation for choice of Bayes ridge estimator; (2) Shared covariance outperforms separate covariance substantially (86.25% vs 82.15% for Llama-8B, Appendix E) suggesting assumption violations not discussed; (3) No threshold selection discussion or sensitivity analysis
Concerning design choice: Figure 3 shows massive prompting variance across different prompt formulations, undermining the motivation that models reliably recognize harmful inputs
Reproducibility concerns: No code release mentioned; exact layer specifications vague; training data composition for prototypes incompletely described

strengths: Well-motivated core insight revealing gap between internal safety understanding and observable behavior (Figure 2), providing compelling justification for the approach
Comprehensive experimental validation across 15 datasets with strong baselines (Aegis, LlamaGuard3, WildGuard) and evaluation spanning 3+ model families with sizes 1B-70B
Practical significance: training-free method addresses real problem of expensive, inflexible guard models; accessible to resource-constrained settings
Model-agnostic design with straightforward extensibility to new threat categories via hierarchical prototypes
Strong empirical results: LPM-M(OLMo2-7B) achieves 89.44 average F1, exceeding WildGuard (88.93) without any training
Thorough ablations on layer depth, sample size, data robustness, and hierarchical variants demonstrating method properties
Good attention to both false positives (true negative rates on neutral datasets) and false negatives (F1 on harmful datasets)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (t-SNE in Figure 1a, scaling curves in Figure 1b)
Reproducibility support: explicit dataset descriptions, hardware specifications, detailed appendix results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies standard prototype-based classification with Mahalanobis distance to LLM representations; technical contribution is incremental rather than introducing new methods or theory
Fundamental dependence on base model quality: method inherits safety limitations from underlying LLM; limited testing on less-aligned models; claim about LLMs encoding safety may not generalize

Significant performance degradation on subtle harmfulness categories (Social Stereotypes 25% error, Sexual Content 19.15% error per Table 5); these are often most important for real-world moderation but lack proposed solutions

Data leakage clarification needed: unclear whether test sets fully held out from prototype computation; suspiciously perfect F1 scores on some datasets (100% on isolated categories) suggest possible evaluation concerns
Multimodal class distributions shown in Figure 1a but addressed only via optional hierarchical prototypes; single mean prototype may be insufficient yet treated as standard approach
Weak theoretical justification for why Mahalanobis distance outperforms Euclidean (9-13% gain in Table 1); brief invocation of high-dimensional properties insufficient
Generalization concerns: evaluation limited to recent well-aligned models (Llama3, Mistral, OLMo2); no evaluation on truly novel threats or older/less-aligned models
Missing analysis of failure modes: Tables 5-6 identify problematic categories but don't explain whether failures are due to annotation ambiguity, representation geometry, or fundamental limitations
Shared covariance assumption (Σ_c = Σ across classes) is practical compromise but suboptimal; Appendix E shows separate covariance underperforms without adequate analysis of why
Incomplete comparison with prompt-based baselines: Section 3.2 shows high variance across 10 prompts, but paper doesn't explicitly demonstrate LPM's consistency advantage
